lead: Some groups of three resistors have three terminals and no pair in series or in parallel. A star (also called Y, wye or T) joins three resistors at one centre node; a delta (Δ, mesh or π) joins three resistors in a triangle. Seen from the three terminals, a star and a delta with the right values behave identically, so one can replace the other. The swap turns a bridge circuit into plain series and parallel parts, and the same idea gives per-phase equivalents of three-phase loads.

sections.h3: Why a three-terminal group blocks reduction

blocks.text: In the bridge of Network terminology, the 10 Ω arm from B to C joins the two halves. No two resistors share one current or one voltage, so series-parallel reduction stops. But the three resistors A-B, B-C and C-A form a delta, and the three resistors meeting at B also form a star. Replacing either group by its other form opens the way to series and parallel steps.

The replacement is equivalent at the three terminals only: the same terminal voltages give the same terminal currents, and the total power entering the group is the same. The currents and powers inside the group are different, so after reducing, go back to the original circuit to find the current in any resistor of the replaced group.

Call the delta resistors R<sub>AB</sub>, R<sub>BC</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>, and the star arms R<sub>A</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>, R<sub>C</sub> from the centre N to the terminals. Matching the resistance seen between each pair of terminals (with the third terminal open) gives three equations whose solution is:
RA = RABRCA/S, RB = RABRBC/S, RC = RBCRCA/S, where S = RAB + RBC + RCA.

Memory rule: star arm = product of the two delta sides that touch that terminal ÷ sum of all three. For example, the pair condition between A and B is RA + RB = RAB ∥ (RBC + RCA); adding and subtracting the three such conditions gives the formulas.

sections.h3: Star to delta, and the balanced cases

blocks.text: Going back, let P = RARB + RBRC + RCRA (the sum of the products taken two at a time). Then RAB = P/RC, RBC = P/RA, RCA = P/RB. Memory rule: delta side = P ÷ the star arm opposite that side (the arm that touches neither of its terminals).

Balanced case: when all three resistors are equal, RY = RΔ/3 and RΔ = 3RY; for example 30 Ω delta sides become 10 Ω star arms. Balanced bridge: if the four outer arms satisfy RAB/RBD = RAC/RCD, then B and C are at the same potential, the cross arm carries no current and can be removed; no transformation is needed. Check for balance first.

examples.question: A delta has R<sub>AB</sub> = 10 Ω, R<sub>BC</sub> = 20 Ω and R<sub>CA</sub> = 30 Ω. Find the equivalent star and convert it back as a check.
steps: R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub>R<sub>CA</sub>/S = 10 × 30/60 = 5 Ω; R<sub>B</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub>R<sub>BC</sub>/S = 10 × 20/60 = 3.333 Ω; R<sub>C</sub> = R<sub>BC</sub>R<sub>CA</sub>/S = 20 × 30/60 = 10 Ω.
R<sub>AB</sub> = P/R<sub>C</sub> = 100/10 = 10 Ω; R<sub>BC</sub> = P/R<sub>A</sub> = 100/5 = 20 Ω; R<sub>CA</sub> = P/R<sub>B</sub> = 100/3.333 = 30 Ω. The delta returns.
examples.answer: R<sub>A</sub> = 5 Ω, R<sub>B</sub> = 10/3 ≈ 3.333 Ω, R<sub>C</sub> = 10 Ω.

examples.question: The bridge in the figure has a 36 V source between D and A, 20 Ω from A to B, 20 Ω from A to C, 10 Ω from B to C, 2 Ω from B to D and 8 Ω from C to D. Find the resistance seen by the source, the source current and the current in each of the three resistors of the delta A-B-C.
steps: Balance check: 20/2 = 10 but 20/8 = 2.5, so the bridge is not balanced and the 10 Ω arm carries current.
Now the path N-B-D is 4 + 2 = 6 Ω and the path N-C-D is 4 + 8 = 12 Ω, in parallel between N and D: 6 × 12/18 = 4 Ω.
Resistance seen by the source: 8 + 4 = 12 Ω. Source current I = 36/12 = 3 A.
Current divider at N: through N-B-D, 3 × 12/18 = 2 A; through N-C-D, 3 × 6/18 = 1 A. With D at 0 V: V<sub>B</sub> = 2 A × 2 Ω = 4 V, V<sub>C</sub> = 1 A × 8 Ω = 8 V, V<sub>A</sub> = 36 V.

Back in the original delta: I<sub>AB</sub> = (36 − 4)/20 = 1.6 A, I<sub>AC</sub> = (36 − 8)/20 = 1.4 A, and I<sub>CB</sub> = (8 − 4)/10 = 0.4 A from C to B. Check KCL at B: 1.6 + 0.4 = 2 A leaves through the 2 Ω.

Power check: the delta absorbs 1.6² × 20 + 1.4² × 20 + 0.4² × 10 = 51.2 + 39.2 + 1.6 = 92 W, and the star absorbs 3² × 8 + 2² × 4 + 1² × 4 = 72 + 16 + 4 = 92 W: same total, different shares. With the 2 Ω (8 W) and 8 Ω (8 W), 92 + 16 = 108 W = 36 V × 3 A.
examples.answer: 12 Ω; 3 A from the source; 1.6 A in A-B, 1.4 A in A-C and 0.4 A from C to B.

traps: Wrong numerator in delta to star: R<sub>A</sub> uses the two sides that touch A (R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>), not R<sub>BC</sub>.
Using the delta sum S as the denominator in star to delta. There the denominator is the single star arm opposite the side.
Reading star-arm currents as the currents of the original delta resistors. Only terminal quantities carry over; go back to the original circuit.
Applying R<sub>Y</sub> = R<sub>Δ</sub>/3 to an unbalanced group. The factor 3 holds only when all three resistors are equal.
Transforming a balanced bridge. If R<sub>AB</sub>/R<sub>BD</sub> = R<sub>AC</sub>/R<sub>CD</sub>, the cross arm carries no current; remove it and reduce directly.

quiz.q: Write the delta-to-star formula for R<sub>A</sub> and the star-to-delta formula for R<sub>AB</sub>.
Why does a star-delta transformation help with a bridge circuit?
quiz.a: The cross arm leaves no pair in series or parallel. Replacing a delta (or star) of the bridge by its other form creates series and parallel pairs, so reduction can go on.

quiz.q: A balanced delta has 45 Ω sides. Find the star arms.
A star has R<sub>A</sub> = 6 Ω, R<sub>B</sub> = 3 Ω, R<sub>C</sub> = 2 Ω. Find the delta.
A Wheatstone bridge has 10 Ω (A-B), 20 Ω (A-C), 15 Ω (B-D) and 30 Ω (C-D), with a 50 Ω galvanometer from B to C. Is a transformation needed to find the resistance between A and D?
quiz.a: No. 10/15 = 20/30, so the bridge is balanced, B and C are at the same potential and the galvanometer carries no current. Remove it: (10 + 15) ∥ (20 + 30) = 25 × 50/75 = 16.67 Ω.

quiz.q: A student uses R<sub>A</sub> + R<sub>B</sub> + R<sub>C</sub> as the denominator in star to delta. Which quick check exposes the error for equal 9 Ω arms?
quiz.a: Equal 9 Ω arms must give 3 × 9 = 27 Ω sides. The wrong formula gives 243/27 = 9 Ω, so the balanced relation R<sub>Δ</sub> = 3R<sub>Y</sub> fails.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power engineers convert delta-connected motor windings and loads to an equivalent star so that one phase can be analysed alone. The same transformation generalises to the star-mesh transformation for a node with more than three branches, and circuit simulators use such node eliminations to shrink resistor networks before solving. Search next for star-mesh transformation and per-phase equivalent circuits.
